stem: Which loop structure is typically used to initialize/traverse every element of a 2D array?

choices.label: B

choices.explanation: While loops CAN be used, but nesting is the key structural idea needed, not specifically "a while loop only".

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nested for loops (one for rows, one for columns)
choices.explanation: An outer loop over rows and an inner loop over columns together visit every element exactly once.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A do-while loop only
choices.explanation: Do-while loops aren't the standard/required pattern for this; nested loops are the key structural idea, not the specific loop type.

explanation: Traversing a 2D array typically uses nested loops: an outer loop for rows and an inner loop for columns.

stem: Which nested loop correctly visits every element of `int[][] arr` with `R` rows and `C` columns?

choices.label: A
choices.text: for (int r = 0; r < R; r++) { for (int c = 0; c < C; c++) { /* use arr[r][c] */ } }
choices.explanation: This correctly iterates r from 0 to R-1 and, for each row, c from 0 to C-1, visiting every element exactly once.

choices.label: B
choices.text: for (int r = 0; r < C; r++) { for (int c = 0; c < R; c++) { /* use arr[r][c] */ } }
choices.explanation: This swaps R and C in the loop bounds, meaning it would use the wrong limits for rows vs. columns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: for (int r = 0; r <= R; r++) { for (int c = 0; c <= C; c++) { /* use arr[r][c] */ } }
choices.explanation: Using <= for both bounds causes out-of-bounds access on both the last row and last column.

choices.label: D
choices.text: for (int c = 0; c < C; c++) { for (int r = 0; r < R; r++) { /* use arr[c][r] */ } }
choices.explanation: This swaps the roles of r and c in arr[c][r], accessing elements with reversed row/column indices.

explanation: The standard nested-loop traversal uses `r < R` for rows and `c < C` for columns, indexing as `arr[r][c]`.

stem: Given a 2D array representing a grid, which nested loop structure prints it row by row, with each row on its own line?

choices.label: A
choices.text: for (int r = 0; r < arr.length; r++) { for (int c = 0; c < arr[r].length; c++) { System.out.print(arr[r][c] + " "); } System.out.println(); }
choices.explanation: The println() is placed after the inner loop finishes, so a newline is printed once per completed row.

choices.label: B
choices.text: for (int r = 0; r < arr.length; r++) { for (int c = 0; c < arr[r].length; c++) { System.out.print(arr[r][c] + " "); System.out.println(); } }
choices.explanation: Placing println() inside the inner loop prints a newline after every single element, not after every row.

choices.label: C
choices.text: for (int r = 0; r < arr.length; r++) { System.out.println(); for (int c = 0; c < arr[r].length; c++) { System.out.print(arr[r][c] + " "); } }
choices.explanation: Placing println() before the inner loop starts prints an extra blank line before each row, rather than after it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: System.out.println(arr);
choices.explanation: Printing a 2D array directly like this doesn't print its contents in a readable grid format; it prints internal reference/type info.

explanation: Printing a newline after the inner loop completes (but inside the outer loop) puts each row on its own line.
